::: {.callout-tip}
## One coherent example

We use six invented shop orders with **distance (km)**, **number of items**, and **fulfilment time (minutes)**. Start the [single-file Python example](../../examples/README.md); this chapter corresponds to `python3 delivery_ml_lab.py geometry`.
:::

## The motivating problem

**What does it mean for two orders or two model directions to be similar?**

Norms quantify size, metrics quantify separation, inner products quantify alignment, and projections find the closest representable point in a subspace. These ideas turn vector operations into geometry; their assumptions matter when features have incompatible units.

## Central mathematical relationship

$$
\operatorname{proj}_{u}(x)=\frac{u^\top x}{u^\top u}u,\qquad (x-\operatorname{proj}_{u}(x))^\top u=0
$$

The equation captures the chapter's principal relationship. Definitions and assumptions are developed in the lessons below; an equation is useful only when the domain and meaning of its symbols are explicit.

## First worked result

Project the feature vector x=(3,1) onto direction u=(1,1). The result is (2,2); the residual (1,-1) is perpendicular to that direction. This same relationship reappears in ordinary least squares and PCA.

## What to pay attention to

A large dot product can reflect long vectors rather than close direction. A geometric interpretation needs a specified inner product and feature scaling.

Read the lessons in sequence, reproduce a calculation by hand, then run the related Python demonstration and explain which mathematical claim the output illustrates. A numerical observation is never, by itself, proof of a theorem.
